logline: A journey from a quiet rented room to St Giles’ great east window, then onward to London’s night skyline: looking up turns a passing visit into a way of paying attention.
theme: Looking up: attention changes the scale of a place.

acts.name: II — The city and the cathedral
acts.beat: The Royal Mile leads into St Giles’, where paintings, glass, and the vault draw the gaze upward.

acts.name: III — The view stays with me
acts.beat: London’s skyline carries that upward pull into the night.

lines.text: I began in Edinburgh, already looking up. Even this ceiling felt like a beginning, right here.
The chair gave me somewhere to land. I sat still before heading out and let my shoulders drop.
Old Town Chambers is at 329 High Street on the Royal Mile. I paused there with my companion.
The Royal Mile, about a Scots mile, links Edinburgh Castle and the Palace of Holyroodhouse. We found our pace.
The street fell behind us as we entered St Giles’.
King David the First founded this church in 1124. Its crown steeple has stood since around 1500.
John Knox preached here from 1559. Today it is Edinburgh's High Kirk, and the quiet pulled my eyes upward.
The great east window sits at the east end of the choir. It shows the Crucifixion and the Ascension.
A guide credits the window to Ballantine of Edinburgh. Its 1874–77 inscription dates mark Falshaw’s term as Lord Provost.
I stood under it longer than I planned.
Below it hang John Bellany's harbour paintings; Port Seton's fishing boats never left his work.
The river held the lights beside me; I stayed still long enough to feel the city slow down.
From the Thames, I spot Viñoly’s 155-metre Walkie-Talkie, completed 2014; upper floors hold the public Sky Garden.
